## Step 2: Refine and qualify the list for LinkedIn outreach


The raw list is not your send list. Founder lists need manual review because a founder can look relevant on paper and be a dead end in practice.


### Remove these before sending


- Solo fitness influencers, personal trainers, or content sites without software
- Agencies that only do marketing for wearable brands
- Sports clubs or leagues themselves — unless your offer serves them directly
- Founders whose company appears inactive: dead LinkedIn page, no recent funding news, no product updates
- Non-founder titles: Head of Partnerships, Growth Lead, etc. Those can be useful later but not for founder-led outreach


### Segment by subvertical


Fitness and sports tech founders don't all share the same pain. Segment by:


- **Wearables / biosensors:** selling to consumers or B2B clinical/human performance buyers, dealing with hardware margins
- **Connected fitness equipment:** selling to hotels, gyms, apartments, or consumers, dealing with long procurement cycles
- **Athlete performance analytics:** selling to teams, universities, or performance directors, dealing with season-based budgets
- **Recovery / wellness tech:** selling to physio clinics, pro teams, or wellness brands, dealing with fragmented buyers
- **Coaching / training platforms:** selling to coaches, academies, or parents, dealing with high churn and low willingness to pay
- **Fan engagement / venue tech:** selling to leagues, venues, or sponsors, dealing with long enterprise cycles


Pick one or two subverticals per sequence. The message to a founder selling wearables into clinical settings should not read like a pitch to a founder selling fan engagement software to venues.


### What "qualified" looks like for this audience


A qualified Fitness and Sports Tech Startup Founder for B2B outreach usually has:


- Founder or co-founder title
- Company size 5–100 employees
- Raised seed, Series A, or later funding — or clearly generating revenue
- Product is B2B or B2B2C, not pure consumer subscription with no B2B motion
- Founder still involved in sales, partnerships, or business development
- Recent activity: hiring a sales lead, launching a pilot program, expanding into a new vertical


If you can't see those signals, the conversation will stall.[Origami](https://origami.chat/) enrichment gives you company size, funding stage, and tools used, so you can filter without leaving the dashboard.


### A simple scoring approach


Score each founder 0–3 on three signals:


1. **Recent trigger:** funding round, hiring post, partnership, product launch — 1 point
2. **B2B motion:** they sell to teams, gyms, clinics, leagues, or venues — 1 point
3. **Founder still selling:** their title or recent activity shows they run sales/partnerships — 1 point


A score of 2 or 3 is worth sequencing. A score of 0 or 1 goes into a nurture list for later.


## Step 3: Create the LinkedIn sequence


You have two ways to build the sequence in[Origami](https://origami.chat/) .


### Option 1: Paste your own templates


Write your own 3-touch sequence and paste the templates directly into Origami's sequencer. Set the delays between touches — Day 1, Day 3, Day 7, or whatever cadence you want — and hit "Launch."


### Option 2: Let the agent write it


Alternatively, you can ask[Origami](https://origami.chat/) 's AI agent to generate a personalized 3-day LinkedIn sequence for all your leads automatically. The agent writes the messages based on each lead's profile data — title, company, industry — so every message feels custom.


Here is a full example sequence you can steal. Replace the bracketed fields with your own details.


### Touch 1 — Day 1: Connection request + note


Subject line: n/a (this is the connection note)


> Hey , saw you're building in . I work with fitness and sports tech founders who sell into gyms, clubs, teams, or leagues and want shorter B2B sales cycles. Noticed on your profile. Worth connecting? I'm not pitching today — just want to follow what you're building and share founder-level outbound notes.


Why this works: it names the niche, signals relevance, and removes pitch pressure.


### Touch 2 — Day 3: Follow-up message (different angle)


Subject line: quick thought on


> Saw your team is hiring a B2B AE — that usually means founder-led sales is hitting the ceiling. Most fitness tech founders I talk to can get demo interest from gyms and coaches, but deals stall because the evaluation process isn't built for short founder cycles. I built to fix that: . Want me to send a 2-minute walkthrough?


Why this works: it references a real trigger (hiring a B2B AE) and names the exact failure mode — interest but no closed deals.


### Touch 3 — Day 7: Final message (soft close)


Subject line: closing the loop


> Last one from me, . If founder-led outbound is still working for , ignore this. But if you want a repeatable way to book demos with gyms, teams, or leagues without adding headcount, is worth a look. Happy to share a short case study from another founder. Open to a 15-minute call next week?


Why this works: it doesn't beg, respects their time, and offers proof without overpromising.


### How to customize these messages without starting over


Three places to personalize:


- ****: funding round, new product launch, hiring post, partnership announcement, recent podcast appearance
- ****: don't say "fitness tech"; say "wearables" or "athlete performance analytics"
- ****: one concrete result your offer delivers — "book 15 qualified gym demos per month" or "cut your pilot-to-close time from 60 days to 30"


If you want[Origami](https://origami.chat/) to do this for you, the agent will pull each lead's title, company, and industry into the message automatically.


### Pre-launch checklist for messages


- Each message under 100 words
- No mention of "I know you're busy"
- One question or CTA max per message
- Reference a specific signal in touch 1 or 2
- No pitch in touch 1


## Step 4: Send the sequence directly from Origami


Here's the part that changes the workflow.


In[Origami](https://origami.chat/) , you launch the sequence directly from the same dashboard where you built the list. No exporting CSVs. No syncing to another tool. No manual copy-paste between LinkedIn and a spreadsheet.


### Launch settings


The built-in LinkedIn sequencer sends connection requests and follow-up messages automatically with the delays you set. For this audience, a cadence of Day 1, Day 3, Day 7 works better than a tight 1-day gap. Founders are busy, and a 2-day gap between touch 1 and touch 2 doesn't feel desperate.


You can also set sending windows to match the founder's time zone. Early morning and late afternoon are usually better for fitness and sports tech founders, but this varies by subvertical.


### Tracking


Opens, clicks, and replies are visible in the same dashboard where you built the list. You click into a contact and you see both their sequence activity and their enriched profile — title, company, tools used. That context matters. When someone replies, you immediately know why you reached out and what angle you used.


### Automatic un-enrollment


If someone replies, they exit the sequence automatically. That prevents the embarrassing mistake of sending a "just bumping this" message after the founder already said yes. The conversation moves to your LinkedIn inbox and you take it from there.


### Cost


The sequencer is included on all paid plans. You're only paying for credits used to enrich leads. The sending itself is free. So once your list is enriched, you can run multiple sequences without multiplying cost per send.


### What response rate to expect for this audience


For a focused sequence targeting Fitness and Sports Tech Startup Founders, I'd expect:


- 25–35% connection acceptance if your own profile clearly speaks to fitness/sports tech and your note references their subvertical
- 8–15% reply rate across the 3 touches if the trigger and offer are specific
- 2–5% positive reply rate — people asking for a walkthrough, case study, or call


Those numbers vary by your offer and founder segment. A founder selling connected fitness into hotels will respond differently than a founder selling athlete performance analytics to universities. Use those ranges as a diagnostic, not a prophecy.


### When to iterate on messaging vs. iterate on the list


- If connection acceptance is under 20%, fix the list or the connection note. The audience may be too broad, or your opening note is too generic.
- If connection acceptance is healthy but replies are under 5%, fix the Day 3 and Day 7 messaging. Try a different angle: hiring trigger, pilot failures, sales cycle length, or investor pressure.
- If replies are healthy but meetings don't show, fix the offer or the calendar flow, not the LinkedIn copy.


Do not rebuild the list every time a sequence underperforms. Change one variable at a time.
